```{r import, include=TRUE}
library(readxl)

### Import CSV file
data1 <- read.csv("/Users/erinanderson/Desktop/R_Work/Stats_HW_1/machine.csv")

head(data1)
```

## a) (2 pts) Use the lm( ) function in R to obtain the estimated regression function.
```{r a, include=TRUE}
lm1 <- lm(minutes ~ machines, data1)
summary(lm1)
```

## b) (3 pts) Using R as a calculator, obtain SSTO.
```{r b, include=TRUE}
# SSTO = summation((y(i) - y(hat))^2)
b1 = 14.7383
b0 = -2.3221
yhat <- b0 + b1*(data1$machines)
ybar <- mean(data1$minutes)
e <- (data1$minutes)-yhat
yi <- b0 + (b1*(data1$machines)) + e
cbind(e, yi)
SSTO <- (yi - ybar)^2
SSTO <- sum(SSTO)
SSTO
```

## c) (3 pts) Using R as a calculator, obtain SSR. You can use the fitted values from the regression in (a).
```{r c, include=TRUE}
# SSR = sum((yhat - ybar)^2)
SSR <- (yhat - ybar)^2
SSR <- sum(SSR)
SSR
```
## d) (3 pts) Using R as a calculator, obtain SSE. You can use the fitted values from the regression in (a).
```{r d, include=TRUE}
# SSE = sum((yi - yhat)^2)
SSE <- (yi - yhat)^2
SSE <- sum(SSE)
SSE
```
## e) (6 pts) Using the pieces above, manually construct the complete ANOVA table for the regression analysis, with columns for Source of variation, SS, df, and MS.
```{r e, include=TRUE}
n <- length(data1$minutes)
MSE <- SSE/(n-2)
MSE
MSR <- SSR/1
MSR
EMSE <- var(data1$minutes)
EMSE
EMSR <- (data1$machines - mean(data1$machines))^2
EMSR <- sum(EMSR)
EMSR <- (b1^2)*EMSR
EMSR <- var(data1$machines) + EMSR
EMSR
```
## f) (2 pts) Obtain the same ANOVA table using R.
```{r f, include=TRUE}
anova_model <- aov(minutes ~ machines, data = data1)
summary(anova_model)
```
## g) (4 pts) Conduct an F test to determine whether or not there is a linear association between time spent and number of machines serviced. Use alpha=0.10. State the null and alternate hypotheses, write your test statistic, rejection region, and p-value. Make a decision, and write your conclusion.
```{r g, include=TRUE}
F <- MSR/MSE
F
#Checking the F table for an F test at alpha = 0.10 with 1 degree of freedom in the numerator and 16 degrees of freedom in the denominator gives a critical F value of 3.29. F* = 805.6 which is greater than the F value allowing us to reject the null hypothesis (H0: beta1 = 0) and accept the alternate hypothesis (Ha: beta1 != 0) that there is a linear relationship between number of minutes spent on a call and number of machines serviced.
```
## h) (2 pts) By what proportion is the total variation in number of minutes spent on a call reduced when the number of machines serviced is introduced as a predictor into the analysis? What is the name of this measure?
```{r h, include=TRUE}
# R^2 is the coefficient of determination which explains the proportion of the total variation of the number of minutes spent on call when number of machines serviced is added as a predictor variable.

R_sqr <- SSR/SSTO
R_sqr

#The total variance explained is 98.05% when number of machines serviced is added as a predictor variable, making the unexplained variance (SSE/SSTO) 1.95%. Adding number of machines serviced in the regression model reduces the unexplained variation in minutes spent on a call by 98.05% 
```
## i) (5 pts) In R, plot the deviations (Yi – Yi(hat)) against Xi on a graph. Plot the deviations (Yi(hat) – Ybar) against Xi on another graph, using the same scales as for the first graph. From your two graphs, does SSE or SSR appear to be the larger component of SSTO?
```{r i, include=TRUE}
# Deviations
SSR_dev <- (yhat - ybar)
SSE_dev <- (yi - yhat)

# Common y-axis scale for both plots
ylim_common <- range(c(SSE_dev,SSR_dev))

# Plot deviations associated with SSE
plot(data1$machines, SSE_dev,
     xlab = "Machines",
     ylab = "Deviations on SSE",
     main = "Residual Deviations",
     ylim = ylim_common,
     pch = 19)

abline(h = 0, lty = 2)


# Plot deviations associated with SSR
plot(data1$machines, SSR_dev,
     xlab = "Machines",
     ylab = "Deviations on SSR",
     main = "Regression Deviations",
     ylim = ylim_common,
     pch = 19)

abline(h = 0, lty = 2)

# SSR appears to be the larger proportion of the deviations on SSTO. 
```
## j) (2 pts) What does this (the SSE vs SSR comparison in part (i)) imply about the magnitude of R2? Explain.
```{r j, include=TRUE}
# Since SSR is much larger than SSE, R^2 is expected to close to 1 (R^2 = SSR/SSTO). A much larger SSR compared to SSE indicates that introducing the number of machines as a predictor explains a large proportion of the total variation in number of minutes spent on a call, leaving very little unexplained variation.
```
## k) (6 pts) Use R to obtain the correlation between the response and predictor variables. Write the steps of a correlation test to see if there is a significant linear association. Using the correlation, calculate your test statistic by hand and find the P-value of the test. Make a decision and write your conclusion.
```{r k, include=TRUE}
# r tells us the correlation and standard version of the slope of the linear regression
r <- sqrt(R_sqr)
r

# The coefficient of correlation (r) is 0.99 indicating a very strong linear correlation between the number of machines serviced and the number minutes spent on a call.

# t = r/sqrt((1-r^2)/n-2)
t <- r^2
t <- 1 - t
t <- t/(n-2)
t <- sqrt(t)
t <- r/t
t

# Checking the t table for the t statistic at alpha = 0.1 on 16 degrees of freedom provides a critical t value of 1.337.The calculated t value (28.39) is much largr than the t statistic (1.337). 

# Calculate two-tailed P-value
p_value <- 2 * pt(-abs(t), df = n - 2)

p_value

# The calculated t value of 28.39 is greater than the critical value of 1.337 and the p value is less than 0.05 (p = 4.087e-15) allowing us to reject the null (H0: rho = 0) and accept the alternate (Ha: rho != 0) and determine that there is a statistically significant linear correlation between the number of machines serviced and the number of  minutes spent on a call.
```
## l) (2 pts) Find the standard deviation of the predictor variable (SX), and the standard deviation of the response variable (SY). Using these quantities, and the correlation, calculate the slope, and confirm that it is the same as you obtained earlier.
```{r l, include=TRUE}
# Sx = sqrt((sum(x - xbar)^2)/n-1)
xbar <- mean(data1$machines)
Sx <- data1$machines - xbar
Sx <- Sx^2
Sx <- sum(Sx)
Sx <- Sx/(n-1)
Sx <- sqrt(Sx)
Sx

# Sy = sqrt((sum(y - ybar)^2)/n-1)
Sy <- data1$minutes - ybar
Sy <- Sy^2
Sy <- sum(Sy)
Sy <- Sy/(n-1)
Sy <- sqrt(Sy)
Sy

# b1*Sx = r*Sy
#b1 = r*Sy/Sx

b1 <- r*Sy
b1 <- b1/Sx
b1

#Check against regression line
summary(lm1)
```
